text: You're climbing a staircase with n steps. Each move, you can go up either one or two steps. How many distinct ways can you reach the top?

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — to reach step i, my last move was either a one-step from i minus one, or a two-step from i minus two. So the count for i is the count for i minus one plus the count for i minus two. Is that the right reading? And are there any constraints on the input size?
Exactly. And n is between one and forty-five.

Got it. With n at most forty-five, the answer stays inside a 32-bit int, so no overflow concerns. Let me run through an example. For n equals three: one plus one plus one, one plus two, and two plus one — three ways. And that's ways of two plus ways of one, two plus one, three. Matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would recurse straight on that formula, but it recomputes the same subproblems again and again — exponential time, two to the n. This problem reminds me of the Fibonacci recurrence: each value is the sum of the two before it, and those subproblems overlap. That's the signal for dynamic programming — fill a table bottom-up, each value once, in linear time. And since each term only needs the previous two, I can drop the array and keep two rolling variables for constant space.

Here's the plan. One: dp of i is the number of ways to reach step i. Two: set dp of zero and dp of one to one. Three: for i from two to n, dp of i is dp of i minus one plus dp of i minus two, and return dp of n. One thing worth flagging — I set dp of zero to one, not zero. That base makes dp of two equal two, which matches the two real ways to reach step two: one plus one, and two. It's the count of the empty climb. And on the sum — it's addition, not multiplication, because I'm splitting the ways by their last move: those two groups don't overlap and together cover everything, so I add. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code it up — and show me the space-optimized version too.

First the straightforward table version: a vector of size n plus one, both bases set to one, then one loop that adds the previous two. And the constant-space version — since only the last two values matter, I roll two variables, prev two and prev one, forward. Both compute the same recurrence. One thing worth flagging — in the rolling version the order of the assignments matters. I compute cur first, then shift prev one into prev two, then cur into prev one. Shift first, and I'd overwrite prev one before using it.

Let's dry-run the table version on n equals five; expected eight. Each entry is the sum of the previous two, so the table reads one, one, two, three, five, eight — the Fibonacci sequence. The row that matters is the last one: dp of five is five plus three, eight. That matches. Corner cases: n equals one never enters the loop and returns dp of one, which is one. N equals two returns two. Both correct.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear for both — a single pass filling n minus one entries. Space is linear for the table version and constant for the rolling version. Oh, one more thing — this is the standard one-dimensional DP template: define the state, write it from the last move, and roll the window when it only depends on a fixed number of earlier terms. Swap the plus for a min and it becomes a minimum-cost climb; allow steps of one, two or three and each term sums the previous three.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You framed the recurrence from the last move and saw the overlapping subproblems that call for DP. You explained why dp of zero equals one is the right base, and why it's a sum, not a product. And you gave the constant-space rolling version with the correct assignment order. Good work.
